text.content: Creating a character for Shadows of The Mandalorian War involves defining their core attributes, skills, advantages, and disadvantages. The process is point-based, allowing for immense customization while ensuring balance. Most campaigns will start with characters between 150-200 Character Points (CP), with Disadvantages typically capped at -40% to -50% of total CP.

Your Game Master (GM) will inform you of the starting Character Point (CP) total for the campaign. This budget determines the overall power and complexity of your character. Higher CP totals allow for more skills, advantages, and higher attribute scores.

Before allocating points, consider the following:

  • Role in the Galaxy: Are you a Republic soldier, a Mandalorian warrior, a budding Jedi, a cunning smuggler, a resourceful technician, or a political operative?
  • Motivation: What drives your character? Personal gain, loyalty, justice, revenge, or a quest for knowledge?
  • Species: Will you play a Human, a Miraluka, a Twi’lek, a Zabrak, or another species? Your choice of species will influence your starting racial traits (advantages, disadvantages, and attribute modifiers).
  • Homeworld (Required): Every character must name a homeworld -- where they were born or spent their formative years, which usually (though not always) sets their native language per @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.aHFgSZUXNODEwQd2]{Chapter 3}. Pick any world from @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.WoKoilSuw4eubRUd]{Chapter 19}’s “Planets of the Old Republic,” a homebrew world of your own at the GM’s discretion, or simply “Unknown” for a character whose origin is murky, forgotten, or deliberately hidden -- a perfectly valid and often thematically rich choice, not a placeholder to fill in later.
  • Dominant Hand (Required): Name the hand your character leads with. It costs nothing and never changes, but every other hand is an off-hand, and weapons held in those take -4 to hit and -1 to parry (see Which Hand Is Dominant, @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.JJ04T5LHImjlILs1]{Chapter 7}). Right is the default for a standard humanoid; left is free, and a species with unpaired or additional limbs names whichever appendage it habitually leads with -- exactly one, however many it has.

Character Creation Steps

Welcome to the heart of character creation! Think of this as telling the story of who your character is. You have a pool of “Character Points” to spend, which is like a budget for buying your hero’s innate talents and abilities. Let’s start with the absolute basics.

Step 1: Define Your Core Being (The Four Attributes)

Everything starts with four core Attributes that describe your character’s raw potential. A score of 10 in any of these is considered the human average.

  • Strength (ST): This is your character’s physical power. It determines how much they can lift, how hard they hit with a melee weapon, and forms the foundation of their physical health.
  • Specialized Strength: Base ST costs 10 Character Points (CP) per level and provides an across-the-board increase to lift, damage, and Hit Points. However, you can save points by purchasing specialized aspects of Strength as separate Advantages during character creation (or with earned CP, pending GM approval). This is ideal for representing specific character concepts, like a massive pack-hauling alien or a lithe, hard-hitting martial artist:
  • Lifting ST (3 CP / level): Increases your ST only for calculating Basic Lift, carrying capacity, and throwing. It does not help you hit harder or take more damage.
  • Striking ST (5 CP / level): Increases your ST only for calculating Thrust and Swing damage for melee weapons and thrown attacks. It does not help you lift heavier objects. Unarmed strikes count: a punch or a kick is a Thrust attack off your ST (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.JJ04T5LHImjlILs1]{Chapter 7}), so Striking ST raises it. Contrast Arm ST below, which reaches punches and grapples but explicitly not kicks.
  • Hit Points (2 CP / level): Directly increases your HP pool for surviving physical damage, representing mass or sheer toughness without adding to lifting power or damage output.
  • Arm ST (5 CP / level for one arm; 8 CP / level for two): Increases ST specifically for actions using your arms (like arm wrestling, swinging a sword, or lifting with those limbs), but does not apply to full-body lifts, Hit Points, or kicks. One arm means one specific arm: only that arm's actions benefit. A two-handed weapon uses both, so it takes the two-arm rate -- there is no half bonus.
  • Size Discount: A positive Size Modifier (SM) gives a 10% discount per +1 SM when buying higher Strength -- base ST, Lifting ST, Arm ST and Striking ST alike -- or Hit Points, reflecting that raw size makes power and toughness cheaper to come by.
  • Fractional SM scales continuously. Unlike standard SM, which is a whole number tied to a fixed height/weight table, this handbook allows fractional SM for species larger than average that don't reach a full size category. SM +0.75 gives a 7.5% discount, SM +1.5 gives 15%, and so on.
  • The discount caps at -80%, for SM +8 or higher.
  • It never applies to a negative SM, or to any attribute or trait other than those listed above.
  • Round the final CP cost down, in the character's favour.
  • It is a rebate for a real cost. A larger character is easier to hit (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.JJ04T5LHImjlILs1]{Chapter 7}) and pays proportionally more for every piece of gear. Smallness carries its own price instead -- reduced Basic Lift (see Size and Basic Lift, below) -- and so takes no CP surcharge.
  • Example: A Wookiee (SM +0.75) with ST 17 is paying for 7 levels above the human average of 10. Base cost is 7 x 10 CP = 70 CP. Applying the 7.5% discount: 70 x 0.925 = 64.75, rounded down to 64 CP.
  • Dexterity (DX): This represents your character’s agility, coordination, and finesse. A high DX makes you a better shot, a more graceful fighter, and skilled with your hands.
  • Intelligence (IQ): This is a measure of your character’s brainpower, awareness, and perceptiveness. IQ governs everything from your ability to learn new skills and solve problems to how well you notice details.
  • Health (HT): This is your character’s physical resilience, stamina, and energy. It dictates how much physical punishment you can endure, how resistant you are to poison and disease, and how long you can keep going before getting tired.

Investing Your Points:

You’ll use your character point “budget” to raise or lower these attributes from the average of 10.

  • Raising or lowering Strength or Health costs or refunds 10 points for each level.
  • Raising or lowering Dexterity or Intelligence is more expensive, costing or refunding 20 points for each level, as they influence a wider range of skills and abilities.

Step 2: Discover Your Derived Abilities (Secondary Characteristics)

Once you’ve set your four core attributes, you can figure out your character’s secondary characteristics. Think of these as the practical, real-world applications of your core potential. By default, they are based on your attributes, but you can spend extra points to fine-tune them, allowing you to create a more specialized character.

Your Survivability & Stamina

Hit Points (HP): This is your life force. It measures how much physical damage you can take before you fall unconscious or die.

  • Default: Your starting HP is equal to your Strength (ST).
  • Fine-Tuning: You can make your character tougher (or more fragile) than their ST suggests by spending 2 points for each extra Hit Point, or gaining 2 points for each HP you give up.

Endurance Points (EP): This is your reserve of raw stamina and grit, used to power strenuous physical activities.

  • Default: Your starting EP is equal to your Health (HT).
  • Fine-Tuning: You can increase or decrease your EP for 3 points per point.

Will: This is your mental fortitude—your courage, focus, and ability to resist intimidation, pain, and temptation.

  • Default: Your starting Will is equal to your Intelligence (IQ).
  • Fine-Tuning: To make your character more mentally resilient (or more easily swayed) than their IQ would indicate, you can spend 5 points per level of Will.

Force Points (FP): For those attuned to the Force, this represents your personal reservoir of energy for using Force powers.

  • Default: Your starting FP is based on your Will score.
  • Fine-Tuning: You can deepen this reservoir by spending 3 points for each additional Force Point. Certain advantages can also increase this total.

Your Senses and Reactions

Perception (Per): This represents your general awareness and your ability to notice things using all your senses. For how range, light, terrain, and elevation affect what you notice, see Sighting: Range, Line of Sight & Elevation (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.JJ04T5LHImjlILs1]{Chapter 7}).

  • Default: Your Perception starts equal to your Intelligence (IQ).
  • Fine-Tuning: You can make your character exceptionally sharp-eyed and observant (or a bit oblivious) by spending 5 points per level of Perception.

Vision, Hearing, Touch, and Taste/Smell: You can further refine your individual senses. Do you have the eyes of a hawk or the hearing of a bat?

  • Default: Each of these senses starts at a level equal to your Perception.
  • Fine-Tuning: You can sharpen (or dull) any of these specific senses for 2 points per level.

Fright Check: This measures how well you hold your nerve when faced with terrifying situations. Making one is a 3d6 roll against your Fright Check score, with whatever modifier the source of the fear states. On a failure you are frozen -- you may take only the Do Nothing maneuver (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.JJ04T5LHImjlILs1]{Chapter 7}) -- until the end of your next turn; on a critical failure you are paralysed with fear for 1d turns. A source of fear that names its own effect uses that instead.

  • Default: Your Fright Check score starts equal to your Will.
  • Fine-Tuning: You can represent a character who is especially brave or cowardly by modifying this value for 2 points per +/-1 bonus.

Your Speed and Movement

Basic Speed: This number determines your reaction time, how quickly you can act in combat, and your base chance to dodge attacks. Your Dodge equals floor(Basic Speed) + 3 (Basic Speed plus 3, dropping any fraction), before modifiers: Combat Reflexes adds +1, encumbrance subtracts its Dodge penalty (see Encumbrance Levels), and Size Modifier does not affect Dodge. Penalties to DX from worn gear (untrained Medium or Heavy armor, Blast pieces, a Carry Frame; see Chapters 3 and 13) apply to DX and DX-based rolls only -- they do not change Basic Speed or Dodge, which are computed from your bought DX.

Calculation: Add your Dexterity (DX) and Health (HT) together, then divide the total by 4.

  • Fine-Tuning: You can directly increase your reaction time. Each +0.25 to your Basic Speed costs 5 points.

Basic Move: This is your ground speed—how many yards or meters you can run in one second during combat.

  • Calculation: Add your Strength (ST) and Dexterity (DX) together, then divide the total by 4 (always round down).
  • Fine-Tuning: You can improve your Basic Move by spending 5 points to increase it by one yard/meter per second.

Basic Lift (BL)

Your Basic Lift (BL) is the maximum weight you can comfortably lift with one hand over your head in one second. It is the foundational number used to calculate all of your carrying capacities and encumbrance limits.

The Standard Formula

To calculate your Basic Lift, multiply your Strength by itself, divide by 5, then multiply by your Size Modifier Multiplier (the table in @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.sM4JaeipflPpOZgw]{Chapter 13} -- see Size and Basic Lift, below). A character at SM 0 multiplies by 1 and can ignore the final step.

  • BL = ((ST × ST) / 5) × SM Multiplier
  • (Note: If the result is 10 or higher, round to the nearest whole number).

Normal ST vs. Lifting ST

While your normal Strength (ST) dictates your baseline, the Lifting ST advantage increases your effective Strength only for the purposes of calculating Basic Lift, determining carrying capacity, and throwing. It does not affect your Hit Points or basic melee damage.

  • If your character has Lifting ST, you add those levels to your base ST before running the formula. The Size Modifier Multiplier still applies at the end:
  • Effective BL = (((ST + Lifting ST) × (ST + Lifting ST)) / 5) × SM Multiplier
  • Example: A character with a base ST of 10 and +2 levels of Lifting ST calculates their Basic Lift as if they had a ST of 12. Instead of a standard BL of 20 lbs, their effective BL becomes 29 lbs. This example assumes SM 0; a Wookiee at SM +0.75 would carry 29 × 1.33 = 39 lbs, and a Gand at SM -1 would carry 29 × 0.7 = 20 lbs.
  • Size and Basic Lift: A creature's leverage scales with its frame, so Basic Lift is multiplied by the SM Multiplier table in @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.sM4JaeipflPpOZgw]{Chapter 13}, the same figure that scales gear weight and cost. Final BL = ((ST + Lifting ST) × (ST + Lifting ST) ÷ 5) × SM Multiplier. A Wookiee at SM +0.75 lifts ×1.33; a Gand at SM -1 lifts ×0.7; a human at SM 0 is unchanged. Round as above. This affects Basic Lift, carrying capacity, encumbrance and throwing only -- ST itself is untouched, so skills, contests, Hit Points and melee damage all read straight off ST regardless of size. A small character who wants to hit as hard as a big one simply buys Striking ST, which is what it is for.
  • Why it mostly cancels: Gear scales by the same multiplier, so a character carrying equipment built for their own size is in the same relative position as anyone else -- a Gand's kit weighs ×0.7 and he lifts ×0.7. Size only bites when a character handles loads built for someone else's frame: human-sized crates, a dropped rifle, a wounded comrade. That is the intended feel, and it is why no Size Discount applies to a negative SM.
  • The Size Discount is compensation, not a bonus: Buying ST is cheaper at positive SM (see Size Discount, above) because being large is a real disadvantage elsewhere -- a bigger target is easier to hit (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.JJ04T5LHImjlILs1]{Chapter 7} adds the target's SM to the attacker's roll), and every piece of armor, clothing and gear costs and weighs proportionally more. A small character pays full price for ST precisely because smallness already pays them back: harder to hit, and cheaper, lighter equipment. The reduced Basic Lift is the one price smallness carries, and the discount is the one rebate size carries.

Standard Basic Lift Table

Here is a quick reference for characters at SM 0 (Humans, Twi’leks, Rodians and most other near-human species). Characters at any other Size Modifier take the value from this table and multiply it by their SM Multiplier -- a Wookiee at SM +0.75 multiplies by 1.33, a Gand at SM -1 by 0.7. See Size and Basic Lift, above.

Encumbrance Levels

The total weight of the armor, weapons, and gear your character is wearing or carrying determines your Encumbrance Level. Higher encumbrance drastically slows your movement and reduces your ability to Dodge attacks.

Encumbrance Levels
Encumbrance LevelMax WeightMove PenaltyDodge Penalty
None (0)Up to 1x BLNoneNone
Light (1)Up to 2x BLMove x 0.8-1
Medium (2)Up to 3x BLMove x 0.6-2
Heavy (3)Up to 6x BLMove x 0.4-3
Extra-Heavy (4)Up to 10x BLMove x 0.2-4

Stacking Move Penalties: Encumbrance is not the only thing that multiplies your Move.

  • One Foot (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.LHqDwyGfdwXUdoZO]{Chapter 5}) halves it
  • Force Stasis halves it for a turn (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.cvf2pB6RpI78AvBt]{Chapter 8})
  • a droid with a damaged or crippled motive system has it halved too (Chapters 7 and 17).
  • your posture does too (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.BUSu7dFLs9IzOvPY]{Chapter 9}): crouching multiplies it by 2/3, kneeling or crawling by 1/3.

Harshest Only: When more than one applies, only the harshest takes effect -- they do not compound. A character at Medium Encumbrance (×0.6) who also has One Foot (×0.5) moves at ×0.5, not ×0.3. A kneeling character at Heavy Encumbrance (×0.4) moves at ×1/3, not ×0.13. This is the same principle as conditional bonuses elsewhere in this book: one channel, one value, the extreme of it.

Order of Operations: Order matters and runs one way: flat bonuses and penalties land on Basic Move first -- the Fine-Tuning above, a leg granting +1 Basic Move -- and the multiplier applies to that total, giving your current Move. So a +1 Basic Move at Heavy Encumbrance is worth +0.4 Move, not +1: your gear makes you faster, and your load slows all of you.

Rounding: Round the result to the nearest whole yard, and never below 1.

The Move 1 Floor: That floor holds however the figure was reached -- flat penalties, the multiplier, or both together -- and it matches the 15× BL carry above, which still leaves you Move 1. A character is never reduced to Move 0 by numbers. Total immobility is a condition and always says so in words: Force Stasis at Adept (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.cvf2pB6RpI78AvBt]{Chapter 8}), a droid's second Motive System hit (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.JJ04T5LHImjlILs1]{Chapter 7}) or crippled leg (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.1ZEtj9W2Z8w75PYC]{Chapter 17}).

Why Not Round Down: Rounding down instead would break two things this book prices: a character at Basic Move 5 -- the commonest human figure -- would gain nothing at any Encumbrance Level from the 5-point Move purchase above, and a Basic Move 4 character at Extra-Heavy would stop dead at a lighter load than the 15× BL case that leaves you walking.

Additional Feats of Strength

Using your Basic Lift (BL), you can determine other physical feats:

  • Two-Handed Lift: You can lift 8x your BL over your head using two hands (takes 4 seconds).
  • Shove / Knock Over: You can shove with a force equal to 12x your BL.
  • Carry on Back: You can carry up to 15x your BL strapped to your back, but you can barely walk (Move 1).
  • Drag / Tow: You can drag an object weighing up to 15x your BL across flat ground.

Size Modifiers represent an object or character’s general size, and by extension, how easy they are to hit. The default Size Modifier is 0, representing human-sized characters (ranging from ~4 ft 4 in to just under 7 ft). A character’s Size Modifier is derived from height by the formula SM = 6 x log10(height in feet / 6 ft), rounded to two decimals -- so 6 ft is SM 0 and every height maps to one exact figure. The table below is a quick visual reference for reading off familiar sizes; for a character’s own SM, and for any height that falls between its rows, use the formula (then apply any shape adjustment, below).

Note: If a creature’s longest dimension falls between two entries, the formula above gives its exact Size Modifier (the table rounds; the formula does not). If a character is box-, sphere-, or blob-shaped, add +2 to their SM. If they are an elongated shape (like most ground vehicles), add +1 to their SM.

A character's body weight is derived, not chosen — it follows from size, Strength, and build. Weight in pounds is 165 × (Height / 6 ft)³ × the Build Multiplier × the Strength Adjustment. The cube term is the figure the Size Modifier already carries: (Height / 6 ft)³ = 10^(SM / 2), so weight reads straight off SM. The anchor is an average-build Human at ST 10 and SM 0: 165 lb (75 kg).

Build Multiplier: Slight ×0.8, Average ×1.0, Heavy ×1.25, Massive ×1.5. Every species has a default build — most Average, heavy-framed species (Wookiees, Trandoshans) Heavy, hulking ones (Dowutin) Massive. A character may take a build other than their species default.

Strength Adjustment: add 3% per point of Strength above the species-typical score, subtract 3% per point below. The species-typical score is 10 plus the racial ST modifier, so an average member — buying no ST above the racial baseline — takes no adjustment and weighs exactly size × build; a stronger individual is heavier on the same frame.

Droids: a droid does not use this formula. Its weight is the sum of its fitted components' masses (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.1ZEtj9W2Z8w75PYC]{Chapter 17}), derived like its other hardware stats. Body weight is descriptive — encumbrance is set by carried gear, not the wearer's own mass — and a very small frame can fall below the formula's realistic floor (a sub-metre being reads implausibly light under pure cube-scaling), in which case the species entry gives a fixed canonical weight instead.

Step 3: Choose Advantages

Select advantages that fit your character concept. These traits cost Character Points. Remember that some advantages, like Force Sensitive, are prerequisites for others.

Step 4: Select Disadvantages

Choose disadvantages to gain back Character Points. These traits hinder your character but add depth and roleplaying opportunities. Your GM will set a maximum value for disadvantages you can take (e.g., -40% of total CP).

Step 5: Buy Skills

Spend Character Points to acquire skills relevant to your character’s background and aspirations. Skills are listed with their controlling attribute and difficulty. (Detailed in @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.aHFgSZUXNODEwQd2]{Chapter 3}: Skills).

Step 6: Flesh Out Details

Give your character a name, a personal history, a distinctive appearance, and personality traits. This makes your character unique and easier to roleplay.

Step 7: Purchase Equipment

Allocate starting wealth to acquire weapons, armor, tools, and other necessary gear. (Detailed in Chapters 10–14: Equipment).

Welcome to the Mandalorian Wars. In an era of total war, your survival depends on your choices, your resource management, and your ability to maintain your gear in the field. Use this guide to prepare your character for the front lines.

Wealth and Starting Credits

Your financial standing is determined by your chosen Wealth trait during character creation. This capital represents your personal funds, savings, and assets available before the campaign begins.

  • The Baseline: Every character starts with 7,000 Credits.
  • Wealth Trait Adjustments:
  • Dead Broke (-25 CP): Reduces starting credits to 0. The character owns only what a template or advantage grants them -- see @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.LHqDwyGfdwXUdoZO]{Chapter 5} for the full disadvantage.
  • Poor (-15 CP): Reduces starting credits to 500.
  • Struggling (-10 CP): Reduces starting credits to 1,900.
  • Comfortable (+10 CP): Increases starting credits to 26,000.
  • Wealthy (+20 CP): Increases starting credits to 100,000.
  • Trading CP for Credits: If you need additional capital, you may trade 1 Character Point (CP) for 700 Credits. This is capped at a maximum of 5 CP total to ensure campaign balance.

Acquiring Your Gear

Purchase your initial weapons, armor, and survival gear from the official equipment tables in the Shadows of The Mandalorian War Handbook.

  • Priority for Survival: The Mandalorian Wars are a brutal, lethal environment. Credits should be prioritized for “Survival” gear—medpacs, breath masks, flares, and environmental protection—rather than purely offensive loadouts.
  • Discouraging CP Purchases: Do not use CP to buy standard equipment found on the tables. Credits are the standard and most efficient way to acquire gear.
  • Strategic CP Spending: Only use CP for:
  • Signature Gear: Items critical to your character’s identity or history. This provides narrative protection, ensuring the item is not permanently lost or destroyed by “bad luck” rolls.
  • High-End Advantages: Use CP to purchase advantages like Gadgeteer[25], or Quick Gadgeteer[50] if you wish to start with experimental, restricted, or advanced tech unavailable through standard purchase channels.

In this setting, there is no such thing as “plug-and-play” augmentation. Cybernetic installations are clinical, invasive, and utilitarian. This is a summary, for full details see @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.o2ZbGiux36xwNCw0]{Chapter 14}: Implants & Cybernetics.

1. Installation and Medical Risks

Whether splicing a neural processor into the brain stem or replacing a limb, all installations are major, invasive procedures.

  • Surgical Requirement: All cybernetics require professional medical intervention in a sterile environment.
  • The Surgeon: A successful Surgery skill roll is required. In the absence of a surgeon, the procedure can be attempted with a penalty using First Aid-12, Physician-5, Physiology-8, or Veterinary-5. A character may only self-operate if they have the Surgery skill and access to an automated medical bay.
  • Surgical Costs: The player must pay the clinic (1,000–5,000 Credits) for every installation or removal.
  • Complications:
  • Failure (Poor Calibration): Hardware is installed but poorly calibrated. Active bonuses are offline until recalibrated by a surgeon.
  • Critical Failure: The patient suffers significant trauma (3d for neural/limbs; 2d for sensory), the hardware is destroyed, and they suffer additional category-specific penalties (e.g., permanent loss of limb function, sensory trauma, or neural shock).

2. Acquisition and CP Cost Structure

Players must spend CP for the traits provided by hardware. When replacing an existing, non-functional cybernetic with an identical one, CP costs are waived—only the Credit cost and recovery time apply.

Calculation Steps

  • Base Limb Status: If replacing a natural limb, or starting with an implant, the player pays the base CR cost of the limb, or implant. If adding an Extra Limb, pay the base CP cost (10 for an arm, 5 for a leg). Note: Extra limbs create new hit locations.
  • Augmentations: Add the CP cost of any internal advantages (e.g., Arm ST, weapon mounts).
  • System Limitations: Sum the total from steps 1–2; this is the printed CP cost of the implant’s granted advantages. The mandatory flaws Electrical [-20] and Daily Maintenance [-10] apply automatically the first time a character installs cybernetics, offsetting this cost. They are applied only once; an identical replacement charges no CP.

3. Mandatory Traits

All cybernetics carry inherent mechanical advantages, and vulnerabilities.

Universal Mandatory Modifiers

  • Striking ST (1 Level, 5 points): Hydraulic actuators or synthetic muscle fibers in an arm or hand. Adds only to damage, not lifting capacity.
  • Lifting ST (1 level, 3 points): Reinforced joints and power-assist skeletal frameworks. Adds directly to carrying capacity, but does not increase striking damage.
  • Electrical (-20 pts): Susceptible to ion/EMP weaponry; can cause structural deactivation.
  • Daily Maintenance (-10 pts): Requires daily upkeep using Armoury, Electronics Repair, or Mechanic skills. Skipping maintenance causes immediate loss of 1 HT, requiring a roll to avoid further loss.

4. The Starting Surgery Exception

For characters created with existing cybernetics, Credit/Surgical fees are waived as “pre-paid” history. Mandatory: The player must account for a recovery period in their backstory, establishing they were “under the knife” prior to the campaign start.
